skills.title: SI Units
skills.summary: The SI system gives everyone the same base units: the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, and the second for time.
objectives: Name the SI base unit for length, mass, and time
Explain why shared units matter

skills.title: Measuring Length
skills.summary: Length is measured in meters and related units. Millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers scale by powers of ten.
objectives: Choose a sensible length unit for an object
Read a length measurement with its unit

skills.title: Unit Conversion
skills.summary: To convert within the metric system, multiply or divide by powers of ten: 1 meter = 100 centimeters, 1 kilogram = 1000 grams.
objectives: Convert between metric length units
Convert between metric mass units

skills.title: Estimation and Reasonableness
skills.summary: Estimation gives a sensible approximate value and helps you check whether a measurement is reasonable.
objectives: Estimate everyday lengths and masses
Judge whether a measurement is reasonable

skills.title: Accuracy and Precision
skills.summary: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. They are not the same.
objectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision
Judge a set of measurements for accuracy and precision

skills.title: Measuring Mass
skills.summary: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured with a balance in grams and kilograms. Mass does not change with location, unlike weight, which depends on gravity.
objectives: Select an appropriate unit and instrument for measuring mass.
Convert between grams and kilograms.
Distinguish mass from weight.

skills.title: Measuring Time
skills.summary: Time is measured in seconds, the SI base unit, along with minutes and hours. Instruments such as stopwatches measure intervals, and careful timing includes repeating measurements because human reaction time introduces error.
objectives: Convert between seconds, minutes, and hours.
Choose an instrument and unit for timing.
Explain why timing measurements are repeated.

skills.title: Measuring Temperature
skills.summary: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is, read with a thermometer in degrees Celsius or in kelvins. Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius, and temperature is distinct from the total heat energy in an object.
objectives: Read and compare temperatures.
Use the freezing and boiling points of water as reference points.
Distinguish temperature from heat.

skills.title: Measuring Volume
skills.summary: Volume is the space a substance occupies, measured in liters and milliliters for liquids or cubic centimeters for solids. Liquids are measured in a graduated cylinder by reading the bottom of the meniscus at eye level.
objectives: Choose an instrument and unit for measuring volume.
Convert between liters and milliliters.
Read a graduated cylinder correctly.

skills.title: Significant Figures
skills.summary: Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that carry real information about its precision. A measurement of 12.5 cm has three significant figures, showing it was read to a tenth of a centimeter; a calculated result should not claim more precision than the measurements it came from.
objectives: Count the significant figures in a measurement.
Explain what significant figures indicate about precision.
Avoid reporting more precision than the data supports.

components.body: Name the SI base units for length, mass, and time.
If everyone measures with different rulers, results cannot be compared. The SI system fixes shared units so a meter means the same thing everywhere.
SI base units: the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, and the second (s) for time.
To report how far a ball rolled, use meters. To report how heavy it is, use kilograms.
SI base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time).
Choose a sensible unit and read a length with its unit.
Small things are measured in millimeters or centimeters; rooms in meters; long distances in kilometers. The unit should fit the size.
1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m. Each step scales by a power of ten.
A pencil is about 18 cm long. A doorway is about 2 m tall. A walk to school might be 1 km.
Pick a length unit that matches the object's size, and always write the unit.
Convert between metric units by multiplying or dividing by powers of ten.
Converting does not change the amount, only the unit. 1 meter and 100 centimeters are the same length written two ways.
Convert 3 m to cm. Since 1 m = 100 cm, multiply: 3 x 100 = 300 cm.
Multiply when moving to a smaller unit (more of them) and divide when moving to a larger unit.
Metric conversions multiply or divide by 10, 100, or 1000; the amount stays the same.
Estimate everyday quantities and check if a measurement is reasonable.
An estimate is a sensible approximate value. It helps you catch mistakes: if a mouse 'weighs' 50 kg, something is wrong.
Estimate the height of a door. A typical door is about 2 m. A '2 km' door is unreasonable.
Estimate to get a sensible ballpark and to check measurements for reasonableness.
Tell accuracy and precision apart and judge measurements by both.
Accuracy is how close you are to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. A measurement can be precise but not accurate.
Think of a target: accurate hits cluster on the bullseye; precise hits cluster tightly together, even if off-center.
components.accessible_text: On a target, accurate shots land near the center; precise shots land close together, which may be away from the center.

components.body: A scale reads 5.0 kg every time for a true 3.0 kg mass. It is precise (same result each time) but not accurate (far from 3.0 kg).
Getting the same answer repeatedly (precision) does not guarantee it is correct (accuracy).
Accuracy = close to true value. Precision = repeatable. They are different.
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to measure and convert mass and explain how mass differs from weight.
Recall the SI system and that metric units are related by powers of ten. The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram.

A balance compares an unknown mass against known masses, which is why it gives the same reading anywhere. An astronaut's mass is the same on the Moon as on Earth, even though they weigh much less there, because weight depends on gravity but mass does not.

Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg) or grams (g), with 1 kg = 1000 g. It is measured with a balance. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass and changes with location; mass does not.
Convert 2.5 kilograms to grams. Since 1 kg = 1000 g, multiply: 2.5 times 1000 = 2500 g.
A sample reads 750 g. In kilograms that is 750 divided by 1000 = 0.75 kg.
A common mistake is treating mass and weight as the same. Mass is the amount of matter and is constant; weight is a force that changes with gravity.
Mass is the amount of matter, measured with a balance in grams and kilograms (1 kg = 1000 g). Unlike weight, mass does not change with location.
Why does an object's mass stay the same on the Moon while its weight changes?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to measure and convert time and explain sources of timing error.
Recall the SI system. Unlike length and mass, time units step by 60 rather than by powers of ten.

A stopwatch measures an interval between two moments. But your thumb does not press exactly when the event happens, so every hand-timed measurement is slightly off. Timing several trials and comparing them shows how large that wobble is.

The SI base unit of time is the second (s). 1 minute = 60 s and 1 hour = 60 minutes. Intervals are measured with clocks and stopwatches. Human reaction time adds error to hand timing, so measurements are repeated.
Convert 3 minutes to seconds. Since 1 min = 60 s, multiply: 3 times 60 = 180 s.
A run takes 120 seconds. In minutes that is 120 divided by 60 = 2 minutes.
A common mistake is converting time as if it used 100 instead of 60, or reporting a single hand-timed value as exact. Use 60, and repeat trials.
Time is measured in seconds (SI base unit), with 60 s per minute and 60 minutes per hour. Hand timing carries reaction-time error, so trials are repeated.
Why should a hand-timed measurement be repeated several times?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to measure temperature, use reference points, and distinguish temperature from heat.
Recall the SI system, and that negative numbers describe values below zero on a scale.

A thermometer is a vertical scale you read directly. A cup and a bathtub of water can be at the same temperature, yet the bathtub holds far more heat energy because there is much more water. Temperature tells how hot, not how much energy in total.

Temperature is measured with a thermometer, commonly in degrees Celsius; the SI base unit is the kelvin (K). On the Celsius scale water freezes at 0 and boils at 100. Heat is energy transferred between objects, while temperature indicates how hot an object is.
A liquid is at 25 degrees Celsius and is cooled by 30 degrees. The new temperature is 25 - 30 = -5 degrees Celsius, below freezing.
Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius and freezes at 0. The interval between these reference points is 100 - 0 = 100 degrees.
A common mistake is confusing temperature with heat. A large object at a low temperature can contain more heat energy than a small object at a high temperature.
Temperature is read with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius (or kelvins), with water freezing at 0 and boiling at 100 degrees Celsius. Temperature is not the same as total heat energy.
What is the difference between temperature and heat?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to measure volume correctly and convert between liters and milliliters.
Recall that the volume of a box is length times width times height, and that metric units scale by powers of ten.

Pouring a liquid into a graduated cylinder, its surface curves. Reading the top of the curve gives a value that is too high, so you read the bottom of the curve, with your eye level with it, to get the true volume.

Volume is the space occupied by matter. Liquids are measured in liters (L) and milliliters (mL), with 1 L = 1000 mL, using a graduated cylinder read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. Solids may be measured in cubic centimeters, and 1 mL equals 1 cubic centimeter.
Convert 2 liters to milliliters. Since 1 L = 1000 mL, multiply: 2 times 1000 = 2000 mL.
A cylinder reads 250 mL. In liters that is 250 divided by 1000 = 0.25 L.
A common mistake is reading the top of the meniscus, or reading from above or below eye level, both of which give the wrong volume.
Volume is measured in liters and milliliters (1 L = 1000 mL) with a graduated cylinder, read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. 1 mL equals 1 cubic centimeter.
Where on the meniscus do you read a graduated cylinder, and from what position?
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to count significant figures and explain why results must not overstate precision.
Recall decimal place value, and that precision describes how finely a measurement was made.
A ruler marked in millimeters lets you honestly report 12.5 cm, but not 12.5432 cm; the extra digits are invented. Significant figures are a way of stating how much of a number you actually know.

Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning about a measurement's precision: all non-zero digits count, zeros between non-zero digits count, and leading zeros do not. A calculated result should be reported to no more significant figures than the least precise measurement used.
How many significant figures are in 12.5 cm? The digits 1, 2, and 5 all carry information, so there are three significant figures, meaning the value was read to the nearest tenth of a centimeter.
How many significant figures are in 0.045? Leading zeros do not count, so only 4 and 5 do: two significant figures.
A common mistake is copying every digit from a calculator. If you measured to three significant figures, reporting eight digits claims precision you do not have.
Significant figures show how precisely a value is known. Non-zero digits and zeros between them count, leading zeros do not, and results must not exceed the precision of the data.
Why should a calculated answer not have more significant figures than the measurements used to find it?
